figures.caption: Figure 4: Proportion of different ML models and runtime decomposition for each agent. Left: Each agent uses one type of ML model for one task, then we report the proportion of different ML models used across all successfully evaluated tasks. Traditional families include boosted trees, forests/ensembles, and linear/baseline models; neural families include MLPs, non-pretrained DNNs, and pretrained/transformer-based large models. Middle: the same breakdown for the fixed DeepSeekV3.2 ablation. Right: wall-clock runtime decomposition for the nine non-search-loop agents, with radial lengths square-root scaled. Agent/LLM time covers non-training interaction, planning, execution, and search overhead, while model-training time is separate from them. MLEvolvege and MLMaster-2.0dv4 are omitted from the right panel because they always run until the time limit 2h.

Table A29: ML-model families in the same-backbone ablation. Cells are task counts among submissions with recorded or recoverable model metadata; n is the number of tasks assigned to a model family. Columns use the same definitions as Table A21. Rows are directly comparable because every method uses the same DeepSeek-V3.2 backend. Figure 4 (middle) visualizes this table in the main text.

Table A13: Failure taxonomy for the main 11-agent leaderboard. The 111 failures are mutually exclusive. Most occur before valid model evaluation, especially missing submissions, rather than from low held-out scores; fixed-backbone variants are analyzed in App. A4.11.

Table A14: Submission, success, and failure breakdown on BioXArena (76 tasks, 11 displayed agents). “Subs” = tasks that produced a submission.csv; “OK” = tasks that also passed the held-out evaluator. The five rightmost columns decompose the remaining failures into mutuallyexclusive categories (definitions in Table A13); their sum equals Fail. “Const. n” and “Const. score” are diagnostics, not part of Fail: they count successful non-Pearson/Spearman submissions whose prediction rows are identical for every test example and report their mean score. GPT-5.4 is the only agent that submits on every task; DeepSeek-V3.2 fails on every axis. Same-backbone DeepSeek-V3.2 variants of Biomnidv3, STELLAdv3, and MLEvolvedv3 are deferred to § 3.4. Figure 3 (c) visualizes these counts in the main text.
Table A24: API pricing. Prices (USD per million tokens) used to estimate $cost per task.

Figure 1: Overview of BioXArena. (a) Tasks are curated from journals, conferences, and public databases by ML and biology experts, then packaged as unified public task capsules with hidden private labels and graders. (b) The resulting benchmark contains 76 tasks across 9 biomedical ML domains. (c) The evaluation covers 11 agents, grouped into closed-source general LLMs, open-source general LLMs, biomedical agents, and ML coding agents. (d) All agents run under the same 2-hour, single-GPU sandbox and submit a submission.csv to held-out task-specific graders. (e) Nine evaluation metrics feed the leaderboard, domain heatmaps, failure taxonomy, and cost analysis.
Table A12: Slurm resource configuration for agent runs and evaluation.

Table 1: Biomedical benchmark comparison. Most biomedical benchmarks fall into two categories: reasoning and coding. The upper rows show biomedical reasoning tasks, while the lower rows present BioML coding tasks involving model training and held-out sample prediction. We report biomedical task counts, domain coverage, per-task input multi-modality (percentage and count), and data sources; superscripts clarify non-obvious counting or subset decisions. Extended benchmark descriptions are given in App. A1, with BioXArena’s multi-modality and multi-source input discussed in App. A2.1.
Table A18: Best and worst domain per agent.
Table A17: Per-domain spread of penalized scores. Chemical-biology is the most discriminative (∆ = 0.54); network-biology is the least (∆ = 0.08).

Table A25: Three-run robustness for general LLM agents. Penalized all-task scores are on the 0–100 scale. Flips count tasks whose pass/fail status changes and are shown in Run 1–2 / Run 1–3 / Run 2–3 order.
Table A19: 10 hardest tasks. Mean normalized score across 11 displayed agents.

Figure 6: Per-task progress during MLEvolvege’s 12 h search. Each line traces the best validation metric found so far for one task during the agent’s internal search. Curves are non-decreasing because only improvements are plotted and then carried to 12 h. Most gains arrive early; the remaining tail corresponds to the hidden-test score improvements in Table 3. Panel (a) shows 8 chemical-biology tasks; panel (b) shows 7 phenotype–disease tasks after one crash before the candidate generation.

Figure 2: BioXArena domain, storage, and input heterogeneity. Left: domain-level composition of the 76 tasks across nine BioML domains, with per-domain task counts and public storage footprints. Right: per-task input-source count versus public-capsule storage size on a log10 scale; colors indicate domains and marker shapes distinguish multi-modal from uni-modal tasks. The domain/task catalogue and modality audit are in App. A2.1, and storage definitions are in App. A2.3 for reference.

Table A21: ML-model families emitted by each agent across BioXArena submissions with recorded model metadata. Cells are task counts; n is the number of tasks assigned to a model family. Top-level split: Classical ML (boosted trees, forest/ensemble methods, linear or constant baselines, and other classical models) vs. Neural architectures (MLP, DNNs without pretrained encoders, and Transformer/pretrained encoders). Figure 4 (left) visualizes this table in the main text. See footnotes for which concrete model classes feed each column.

Table A22: ML-model families emitted per domain, summed across the 11 displayed agents. Same column families and footnote conventions as Table A21; n is the total number of (agent, task) pairs with a model-family assignment in that domain (out of 11× 8–10 = 88–110).

Table A15: Full per-agent statistics for the 11 displayed agents. “Succ. mean” averages normalized score over successfully evaluated tasks, while “Penalized” averages over all 76 tasks with failed runs scored as zero. Avg time is the total wall-clock average over all 76 task outputs, using outer runner elapsed time when available and falling back to runner-injected code_total_time_sec or failed-attempt durations when needed. Multi-round tasks contribute once: the first successful run if any run succeeds, otherwise the last failed run among the official merged rounds. The “In tok” and “Out tok” columns are per-task averages: cumulative LLM API tokens within the selected task outputs divided by 76 tasks; for search agents, this includes all recorded planning, review, improvement, and repair calls. MLEvolvege is therefore much more LLM-token-heavy than MLMaster-2.0dv4, whose search spends more of the 2 h budget in local code execution and hyperparameter/model trials. Cost is computed from the token counts at provider-published prices checked on May 1, 2026 (see Table A24).
Table A16: Mean normalized score per agent × domain. Cells show the penalized average over all tasks in that domain. Bold marks the per-domain leader.

Table A27: Failure breakdown for the same-backbone ablation. All five rows use DeepSeek-V3.2 as the backend LLM. Columns use the same mutually-exclusive failure categories as Table A13; the five category columns sum to Fail. Compared with the bare DeepSeek-V3.2 code-extract loop, specialised scaffolds primarily reduce missing-submission failures, while STELLAdv3 remains dominated by ID-mismatch errors. Figure 5 (c) visualizes these counts in the main text.
Table A26: Constant-prediction submissions. Non-regression submissions that passed evaluation. Scores are normalized task scores.
Figure 7: Violin plots show normalized scores on 10 tasks for the top four agents from main experiment and human experts. Dots are individual tasks; black bars mark the average score.
Table A31: Human–agent comparison. Normalized hidden-test scores on the 10-task pilot for human experts and four leading agents. The bottom row reports mean ± sample std over the 10 tasks.
Table A11: Grading functions used by BioXArena evaluators.

Table A23: Cost and efficiency of the 11 displayed agents. The left wall-clock block averages over successful tasks; the right block averages over all 76 tasks. When a task is run in multiple rounds, it contributes once: the first successful run (round_succeeded) if any run succeeds, otherwise the last failed run among the official rounds_used. Totals use the outer runner elapsed time when recorded, falling back to runner-injected code_total_time_sec or failed-attempt durations when needed. Agent/LLM is non-training wall-clock, including API interaction, reasoning, wrapper execution, and search when phase separation is unavailable; Train is the model-training time when separately logged. “Total tokens” reports the run-level sum of input+output tokens over the selected one output per each of the 76 tasks, not a per-task average; Table A15 reports the corresponding per-task averages. For search agents, these totals include all recorded planning, review, improvement, and repair calls. “$/task” divides the corresponding total token cost by 76 tasks and uses published API prices checked on May 1, 2026 (Table A24). Figure 4 (right) visualizes the all-task timing columns.
